threads.thread_goal: Align on campaign objectives, target segments, and value proposition

messages.text:
Sharing a first rough draft of the campaign brief for the new printed catalog service, based on A1 and the scope in T1.

Proposed primary objective: generate qualified catalog quote requests via the landing page form, within the 21-day launch window.

Initial thought on KPIs: number of quote requests, cost per quote request, and conversion rate from visit to form submit. I have not yet tied these to specific numeric targets.

Target segments I am considering:
- Existing small and mid-size ecommerce brands that want a physical catalog to support repeat orders
- Local retailers that need seasonal catalogs for in-store distribution

Value proposition draft: 'Customized printed catalogs that make your products tangible, with print quality that matches your online brand and fast turnaround.'

This is still early. Can you all take a look and react, especially on whether these objectives and segments feel right before I finalize A1 and move deeper into T2?

Thanks for kicking this off. From what we hear on calls, the ecommerce brands segment definitely resonates. They often ask how to showcase bestsellers in a more tangible way for repeat buyers.

For local retailers, I wonder if we should narrow further, maybe focus on those with at least a basic online presence so the online-to-offline flow makes sense.

On the objective, could we add something around quote quality, not just volume? For example, ensuring the requests include enough spec detail so sales does not spend time chasing basics.

Happy to help refine the value prop so it lines up with what we can confidently say on calls and in A4 later.

From the production side, the objective and segments look generally workable, but I would tweak the value prop so it does not overpromise on turnaround.

For example, instead of 'fast turnaround' as a blanket statement, we could say something like 'reliable turnaround with clear timelines' and then specify typical lead times by catalog size and finish in the detailed copy.

Also, for A1 it would help if we already flag which catalog formats we want to push hardest at launch: page ranges, paper types, and finishes that we can produce consistently without bottlenecks. That will later feed into A3 and T3.

If we align that early, we reduce the risk of misalignment between the online offer and what we can actually print.

On the sales side, I like the focus on quote requests as the main objective. To make it more concrete for T1, could we set a target range, even if we refine later once T2 and T7 are clearer?

For example, something like: 'Generate 80–120 qualified quote requests in the first 30 days, with at least 70 percent including basic spec details (format, page count, quantity).'

For segments, I agree with prioritizing ecommerce brands. For the second segment, maybe 'growing regional retailers with multi-store presence' rather than all local retailers. That is closer to the profiles that usually have budget for catalogs.

If we agree on that direction, I can already start thinking about how A4 and A6 should reflect these segments.

From my calls, smaller shops sometimes get confused by technical terms. If we go with ecommerce brands and regional retailers, can we keep the landing page language simple and avoid too many print specs up front?

Maybe we can ask for basic info first and then we clarify details during follow-up. That might help form completion, even if we then need a good structure in A4 to guide the conversation.

I am not sure how that affects the KPIs you mentioned, but I want to avoid forms that feel too complex.

Good point on the turnaround claim. I will remove 'fast turnaround' from the high-level value prop in A1 and instead position it as 'clear timelines and consistent quality', then we can detail typical lead times in the landing page brief and in A3.

On formats, could you suggest 2–3 catalog configurations that are safest to promote at launch? For example, a standard A4, a smaller booklet, etc. Once we have that, I will reflect it in T1 and make sure T4 copy stays within those boundaries.

For launch, I recommend we highlight three catalog types that are straightforward for us operationally:

1) A4, 32–64 pages, matte coated paper, standard binding.
2) A5, 24–48 pages, silk coated paper, standard binding.
3) Slim product booklet, 12–24 pages, lightweight paper, staple binding.

These are stable in our current workflow and easy to proof. I will document these as the primary launch formats in A3 and T3, and we can reference them in A1 as the default options.

That should also help sales when they scope jobs later in A4 and T5.

On numeric targets, I hesitated to lock them too early, but your suggestion is helpful. How about we set an initial objective in A1 as:

'Generate 100 qualified catalog quote requests in the first 30 days post-launch, with at least 70 percent including basic spec details (format, page count, quantity).'

We can then track this via T7 and refine in T10 and T12 once we see actual performance.

For segments, I am hearing consensus around:
1) Ecommerce brands (small and mid-size) with repeat customers.
2) Growing regional retailers with multi-store presence and at least a basic online presence.

If no one objects, I will update A1 and T1 with this framing.

The objective and segments as you phrased them work for me. The volume target feels ambitious but realistic if the media plan in A2 supports it.

On the value prop, could we also mention that the catalogs are tailored to their product mix, not just generic templates? That is something prospects react well to when we talk about printed materials.

As long as we do not imply custom design services beyond what we actually offer, I think that will strengthen the message.

I am aligned with the objective and the two segments you summarized.

On the form and quote quality: to support the 70 percent spec completeness target, we can design the form so that format, page count, and quantity are required fields, but we keep the wording simple as suggested earlier.

Later, in T6 and A6, we can define how sales follows up when specs are incomplete, so we still move those leads forward without too much friction.

From my side, I am comfortable using this as the basis for the sales playbook in T5.

If we make those fields required, can we add short helper text or examples so people know what to put in? For instance, 'A4, 32 pages, 500 copies'.

That would make it easier for me and others when we call them back, because we will have a clearer starting point.

Otherwise I am fine with the objective and segments you all outlined.

From production, I am comfortable with the objective and the two priority segments as long as we keep the promoted formats to the three catalog types I listed earlier.

On the value prop, I suggest we lock the phrasing as something like: 'Customized printed catalogs aligned with your brand, with clear timelines and consistent print quality.' That stays within what we can reliably deliver.

If we agree, I will reflect this wording in A3 and make sure T3 and T8 checks look for any deviations in creatives or copy.

Thanks all, this is very helpful. Let me summarize where we are and check that we are ready to lock this for A1 and T1.

Objective: 'Generate 100 qualified catalog quote requests in the first 30 days post-launch, with at least 70 percent including basic spec details (format, page count, quantity).'

Primary KPIs: quote requests, cost per quote request, visit-to-form conversion rate, and spec completeness rate. We will track these via T7 and later T10 and T12.

Priority segments for launch:
1) Small and mid-size ecommerce brands with repeat customers.
2) Growing regional retailers with multi-store presence and at least a basic online presence.

Value proposition direction: 'Customized printed catalogs aligned with your brand, with clear timelines and consistent print quality,' plus a mention that catalogs are tailored to their product mix, without implying full custom design services.

If there are no strong objections in the next few hours, I will treat this as our baseline and update A1 accordingly.

The summary matches what we discussed. From my side, I am good to proceed with that objective, KPIs, and the two segments.

This will give us a clear frame for the sales conversations and for the FAQ in A4.

Aligned here as well. Locking those two segments for launch will help us focus the sales playbook and training.

I will start drafting segment-specific talk tracks in T5 based on this.

No objections from production. The objective and KPIs are workable, and the segments and value prop are compatible with our current print capabilities.

I will make sure A3 and T3 reflect the three recommended catalog formats so everything stays consistent.

Great, thanks for confirming. I will update A1 today with the agreed objective, KPIs, segments, and value prop direction, and mark T1 as nearly complete pending marketing manager sign-off.

Next I will move on to T2, using these segments and KPIs as the basis for the media plan.

threads.thread_goal: Lock channel mix, budget split, and launch timeline

messages.text:
Following up on the agreed objectives and segments in A1, I have put together a first pass of the media plan in A2 for T2.

Proposed channel mix and rough budget split (within our cap):
- Paid social (Meta + Instagram): 45 percent
- Paid search (brand + non-brand): 35 percent
- Email to existing database: 10 percent (no extra media cost, just production)
- Retargeting display: 10 percent

The idea is to lean on paid social for ecommerce brands and use search to capture intent around printed catalogs and product catalogs.

For timing, I am proposing we go live in 14 days from today. That gives us time to finalize creatives (T4), tracking (T7), and QA (T8, A5) while still staying within the 21-day window.

Would love your thoughts on whether this mix and timeline feel realistic, and if there are any sales or production constraints I should factor in before we lock D3 and D4.

From a sales perspective, the 14-day timeline is fine as long as we can complete T5, T6, and T9 before launch or at least have the essentials ready.

On channel mix, I like the emphasis on paid social for ecommerce brands. For regional retailers, search might be more important, since many of them look for catalog printing when they are already planning a campaign.

Would it make sense to shift a bit more budget into search, maybe 40 percent, and slightly reduce retargeting at the start until we have enough traffic?

Agree with the 14-day target if we lock the training date soon. For T9, I would prefer to run the main session 2–3 days before launch so the content is fresh.

On channels, could we also consider a small test within email for a more consultative angle, like inviting existing customers to a short call about how catalogs can support their current online sales? That might not need extra budget but will affect how we plan T6 and A6.

For D3, I am comfortable with the overall mix but would support a slight increase in search as suggested.

From production, the 14-day go-live is workable if we lock the final creative specs in A3 at least 7 days before launch so T8 QA is not rushed.

One concern: if paid social drives a lot of volume quickly, we need to be sure the lead handling workflow in T6 and the SLA matrix in A6 can absorb it without overpromising on delivery dates.

I would also like to schedule a small test traffic window 1–2 days before full launch to validate tracking (A7) and check that all print claims in creatives match A3 and A5.

For the timeline, I just want to make sure we have enough time to practice the new scripts from A4 before we start getting leads.

If the main training is 2–3 days before launch, could we also share a short summary or cheat sheet earlier so people like me can review it at our own pace? That might not affect D4 directly but will help us be ready when the media goes live.

Good feedback on search. I can adjust the proposed split to:
- Paid social: 40 percent
- Paid search: 40 percent
- Email: 10 percent
- Retargeting: 10 percent

This keeps retargeting small until we have enough volume and gives search more weight for those high-intent queries.

On the 14-day timeline, I will map key milestones in A2 and A7: finalizing creatives (T4), tracking setup (T7), QA (T8), and sales training (T9). I will also add a soft-launch day for test traffic as suggested.

The updated split looks better to me. With 40 percent in search, we can cover both generic catalog printing terms and more specific queries from ecommerce brands.

For email, I suggest we focus on existing customers who already trust our print quality, and position the catalog as an extension of their current materials. That should help with early traction without extra spend.

I am aligned with the revised channel mix.

On the timeline, if we set launch for 14 days from now, I propose we tentatively schedule the main training session (T9) for day 11, with a short async summary shared by day 9 so people can review in advance.

That way, even if someone cannot attend live, they will have A4 and A6 plus the summary to fall back on.

The updated mix works for production as well. The key for us is that creatives for each channel respect the same print claims and formats defined in A3.

For the soft-launch test, I suggest we run a small portion of the budget (for example, 10 percent of daily spend) for 24 hours across social and search, then use A5 and A7 to check tracking, forms, and any print-related statements.

If we do that on day 13, we still have a buffer to fix issues before the full go-live on day 14.

Let me summarize the proposal so we can confirm D3 and D4.

Channel mix and budget split:
- Paid social: 40 percent
- Paid search: 40 percent
- Email to existing customers: 10 percent
- Retargeting display: 10 percent

Launch timeline:
- Today: align on plan.
- Next 7 days: finalize creatives (T4) and specs (A3, T3).
- By day 10: tracking and UTM setup (T7, A7) completed.
- Day 9: share async sales enablement summary (A4, A6).
- Day 11: live sales training session (T9).
- Day 13: soft-launch test with limited spend and full QA using A5.
- Day 14: full campaign launch (T10) and start of 72-hour monitoring.

If this works for everyone, I will update A2 and T2 accordingly and treat day 14 as the official go-live date within our 21-day window.

The summary looks solid. I am comfortable confirming both the channel mix and the day-14 launch date.

This gives us enough time to prepare on the sales side and still move quickly.
Agreed. I will plan T5, T6, and T9 around this schedule and make sure the training and workflow details are ready before the soft-launch test.
Confirmed from production as well. I will align T3 and T8 milestones with this plan and prepare for the soft-launch QA on day 13.

Thanks all. I will update A2 with the confirmed channel mix and day-14 launch date, and adjust T2, T7, and T10 timelines to match.

I will also flag this plan to the marketing manager for final approval on the budget split.

threads.thread_goal: Validate creative concepts against print capabilities and finalize specs

messages.text:
I have reviewed the early creative mockups and the current draft of A3, and I want to walk through a few points before we finalize specs for T3 and T4.

Overall, the concepts look strong, but I see three areas we should adjust:
1) Some social ads mention 'same-week delivery' for all catalogs. That is only realistic for the slim booklet format at certain quantities.
2) A few visuals show foil stamping and embossing, which we can do, but not at the turnaround implied in the copy.
3) The landing page draft references 'any paper type you want', which is too broad.

I propose we tighten A3 so we clearly define which features we can promote in ads and on the landing page, and then update the creatives accordingly.

Sharing this here so we can align before I lock A3 and we move into T8 QA later.

Thanks for flagging these. I had used some generic catalog copy as a starting point and did not fully align it with our actual print capabilities yet.

On delivery, I can adjust the ad copy to talk about 'clear timelines and reliable delivery' instead of 'same-week delivery' and only mention faster turnaround where you confirm it is safe.

For foil and embossing, would you recommend we remove those visuals entirely for launch, or can we keep them with more precise wording? I want to make sure A1 and A3 stay consistent.

I will also revise the landing page brief in T4 so it lists the three main catalog formats you suggested earlier, rather than 'any paper type you want'.

From sales calls, when we mention special finishes like foil or embossing, prospects often assume they are standard and fast. That can create tension later.

For launch, I would prefer we focus the ads and landing page on the core formats and finishes that we can deliver quickly and consistently. We can still mention that additional finishes are available on request during the sales conversation and in A4.

That should keep expectations realistic and make T5 and T9 easier.

I agree with keeping the launch message focused. If we overemphasize special finishes in ads, we will get a lot of questions about pricing and timing that are hard to answer quickly.

In A4, we can include a short section on 'premium options' that sales can bring up selectively once we understand the customer needs and timeline.

For the landing page, maybe we can add a simple note like 'Ask us about premium finishes such as foil or embossing' without promising specific turnaround.

I like the idea of a small note about premium options. On calls, it helps to have something to point to if customers ask about more advanced finishes, but I do not want them to think everything is included by default.

If A4 can give us a simple way to explain the difference between standard and premium options, that would be great.

On foil and embossing, my recommendation for launch is:

- Ads and hero visuals: stick to standard finishes only.
- Landing page: one short line about premium finishes available on request, without images that imply they are standard.

That way, A3 can clearly state that premium finishes are not part of the default offer and should not be used as primary visuals.

For delivery claims, we can safely say:
- Standard catalogs: typical lead times by format and quantity (which I will list in A3).
- Slim booklets: we can mention faster turnaround for certain quantities, but I will specify the conditions so T4 and T8 can check against them.

Understood. I will update the creative brief in T4 so that:

- Ads only show standard finishes and do not mention foil or embossing.
- The landing page has a small 'premium options on request' note without visuals that could mislead.
- Delivery language follows the lead times you will define in A3.

Once you finalize A3, I will share the updated copy drafts here for a quick check before we move to T8 QA.

I have now updated A3 with:

- The three primary catalog formats and their standard specs.
- Clear lead time ranges by format and quantity.
- A section stating that premium finishes (foil, embossing, etc.) are available only on request and should not be promoted as standard in ads.

For T3, this means our creative requirements are now:
- All ad and email visuals must use standard finishes only.
- Any mention of turnaround must match the ranges in A3.

If we agree, I suggest we treat this as our final creative and print specification guideline for launch.

The updated A3 approach works well for sales. Focusing on standard formats and finishes in ads will keep expectations clear, and we can introduce premium options later in the conversation.

I am comfortable with this as the guideline for what we promote in ads and on the landing page.

Aligned here as well. I will make sure A4 and T5 reflect the distinction between standard and premium options, and that we do not promise anything in scripts that is not covered in A3.

This will also help when we prepare the FAQ for T5.

Thanks for clarifying. Having that clear split in A4 will make it easier for me to explain options without overcommitting.

I am fine with using the updated A3 as our reference for what we can say in calls.

Great, I will now revise the ad, email, and landing page copy in T4 to fully align with the final A3 guidelines.

Once the new drafts are ready, I will share them and then we can plan T8 QA using A5 to double-check that all print claims and visuals match what we just agreed.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize sales playbook, lead workflow, and training approach

messages.text:
I have drafted the first version of the sales playbook and FAQ in A4 and the lead handling workflow in A6, based on T5 and T6.

Key elements in A4:
- Opening pitch tailored to the two priority segments (ecommerce brands and regional retailers).
- Discovery questions focused on catalog purpose, product mix, and timing.
- Simple explanation of standard vs premium finishes, aligned with A3.
- FAQ with 18 questions covering pricing, lead times, and file requirements.

In A6, I outlined lead routing rules and response time targets:
- All catalog leads from the landing page form go into the CRM with a 'Catalog' tag.
- Leads are auto-assigned based on region.
- Target response time: first contact within 4 business hours during weekdays.

I would like your feedback before we lock D7 and D8 and schedule T9 training.

Thanks for pulling this together. I went through A4 and A6.

On the playbook, I like the structure and the discovery questions. For ecommerce brands, could we add one more question about how they currently promote repeat purchases, so we can link catalogs to their existing flows?

On response times, 4 business hours is reasonable, but we should clarify what happens with leads that come in late in the day or over the weekend. Maybe we can define a latest next-business-day time in A6 so expectations are clear.

I read the draft A4 as well. The scripts are helpful, but I found some of the wording a bit formal.

Would it be possible to add a shorter version of the opening pitch that we can use on quick calls? Something like a 2–3 sentence version.

On A6, I am fine with the routing by region. It would help to have a simple visual or step list in the training so everyone understands what happens after the form is submitted.

From production, I checked A4 for technical accuracy.

A few small points:
- In the FAQ, one answer suggests we can always accommodate last-minute changes after proof approval. That is risky; we should state that changes after proof approval may affect timelines and cost.
- For file requirements, it would be good to mention that we prefer print-ready PDFs with embedded fonts and images, and that we can support basic checks but not full redesign.

If we adjust those, A4 will be well aligned with A3 and our actual workflow.

I reviewed A4 and A6 from a marketing and funnel perspective.

The opening pitch lines up well with the value prop in A1. I suggest we add a short section on how reps should reference the online campaign when talking to leads, so customers feel a consistent story from ad to call.

For A6, could we also include a simple field mapping from the landing page form (T4) to the CRM fields, so we avoid any confusion when we set up tracking in T7?

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

I will update A4 to:
- Clarify that changes after proof approval may impact timelines and cost, and that we will confirm feasibility case by case.
- Specify that we prefer print-ready PDFs with embedded fonts and images, and that we can help with basic checks but not full redesign.

I will also add:
- An extra discovery question for ecommerce brands about how they drive repeat purchases.
- A shorter, 2–3 sentence version of the opening pitch for quick calls.
- A short note on referencing the online campaign in conversations.

For A6, I will clarify weekend and late-day leads and add a simple field mapping from the landing page form to CRM.

Those updates sound good.

On response times, I suggest we define in A6:
- Leads received up to 3 p.m.: first contact within 4 business hours.
- Leads received after 3 p.m.: first contact by 11 a.m. next business day.
- Weekend leads: first contact by 11 a.m. on Monday or next business day.

If we agree, we can use these as our standard SLAs for D8.

I am comfortable with those response time targets. They are clear and manageable.

The shorter pitch and the FAQ changes you mentioned will also help a lot in day-to-day calls.

The planned changes to A4 address my concerns. As long as we clearly state that post-proof changes may affect timing and cost, we will avoid misunderstandings.

From production, I am fine with the updated A4 and the SLA structure you are proposing in A6.

Once you incorporate these updates, I think A4 and A6 will be in good shape.

For T9, I suggest the training agenda covers:
- Walkthrough of the playbook structure and key messages.
- Role-play of the short opening pitch for each segment.
- Review of the lead workflow in A6, including examples of weekday and weekend leads.

If that works, we can treat the updated A4 structure and the SLA rules in A6 as final for launch.

I have now applied the changes to A4 and A6 as discussed.

To summarize:
- A4 includes segment-specific pitches, an extra discovery question for ecommerce brands, a short pitch version, and clarified sections on premium finishes and post-proof changes.
- A6 defines routing by region, the field mapping from the landing page form, and the response time rules you suggested.

Unless there are further concerns, I propose we confirm this playbook structure and these SLA rules for launch.

I am aligned with the updated A4 and A6. The structure and messaging in the playbook feel practical, and the SLA rules are clear.

From my side, we can confirm these for launch.

Confirmed here as well. The shorter pitch and the FAQ examples make it easier to use in real calls.

Looking forward to the T9 training to practice the flow.

No further comments from production. The updated A4 and A6 are consistent with A3 and our operational constraints.

I am comfortable treating them as final for launch.

Great. With A4 and A6 confirmed, I will make sure the landing page form fields in T4 and the tracking plan in T7 match the workflow.

We can now proceed to schedule T9 on the agreed date and share the materials with the team.

threads.thread_goal: Review early performance, customer feedback, and next optimizations

messages.text:
We are 5 days post-launch, and I have drafted the initial post-launch report in A8 based on T10 and early inputs for T11 and T12.

Headline metrics so far (first 5 days):
- 420 landing page sessions.
- 46 catalog quote requests (on track but slightly below the linear path to 100 in 30 days).
- Visit-to-form conversion rate: 10.9 percent.
- Spec completeness (format, page count, quantity filled): 63 percent, a bit under our 70 percent target.

Channel-level view from A7:
- Paid social: higher volume but lower conversion rate.
- Search: lower volume but stronger conversion and better spec completeness.

I would like to hear from sales on the quality of the first leads (T11) and from production on any issues with expectations so far, then we can agree on the next optimization steps for T12.

On the sales side, we have spoken with 9 of the first 10 catalog leads and have notes ready for T11.

Qualitative observations:
- Ecommerce brands: generally good fit, they understand the value of catalogs and have clear product ranges.
- Regional retailers: more questions about how catalogs fit into their current promotions, but still promising.

Spec completeness: when the form is filled properly, the conversations move quickly. When specs are missing, we spend the first part of the call clarifying basics.

I think we can improve the helper text on the form to nudge better inputs, which should help us reach the 70 percent target.

From my calls, I noticed that some leads are not sure which of the three catalog formats to choose. They sometimes pick 'other' and write something vague.

When that happens, I have to explain the options from A4 again on the call.

Maybe we can tweak the form labels or add a short description for each format so people can choose more confidently. That might also help with spec completeness.

From production, the first proofs and jobs coming in are within our expected range.

A couple of points:
- Some leads are asking for premium finishes right away, even though the ads do not highlight them. It seems they are reading the small note on the landing page and focusing on that.
- A few customers expect faster turnaround than what we list in A3, likely because they are comparing us to digital-only materials.

So far we have managed expectations, but for T12 I would recommend we slightly adjust the landing page copy to make standard lead times more prominent and the premium options note more clearly 'on request and subject to timelines'.

I have compiled notes from the first 10 customer conversations for T11.

Key themes:
- Many ecommerce brands like the idea of using catalogs for loyal customers or wholesale partners.
- Several leads asked for examples of successful catalog campaigns in their sector.
- Questions about minimum order quantities and reprint options came up frequently.

These insights suggest we might want to add a couple of examples or short case-style snippets to the landing page and A4, and clarify minimums and reprints more prominently in the FAQ.

Thanks for the feedback.

On spec completeness and format confusion, I can propose the following quick optimizations for T12:
- Update the form helper text with concrete examples (for example, 'A4, 32 pages, 500 copies').
- Add a one-line description under each of the three catalog formats, using the wording from A3.
- Make the standard lead time ranges more visible on the landing page, and move the premium finishes note further down with clearer 'on request' language.

On the media side, I can also shift a bit more budget toward search, since those leads seem to have clearer intent and better specs so far.

Those changes would help a lot.

On the examples side, even a short paragraph on the landing page describing how an ecommerce brand used catalogs for repeat buyers would give us a good reference point in calls.

For media, I support a modest shift toward search while we monitor how social performs after the copy tweaks.

The helper text and format descriptions would make my follow-up calls smoother, since customers would already have a clearer idea of what they want.

If we can also add a short note about minimum order quantities on the form or confirmation email, that might reduce one of the common questions we get.

I support making standard lead times more prominent and moving the premium finishes note further down.

For A3 and A8, I can provide a short table summarizing typical lead times and minimum order quantities by format. You can then reuse that table in the landing page and in A4.

That should help align expectations and reduce back-and-forth on basic specs.

I will update A4 to:
- Add a couple of short example scenarios (for instance, a brand using catalogs for wholesale partners).
- Highlight minimum order quantities and reprint options more clearly in the FAQ.

I will also incorporate any lead time and minimum order tables that 64810 provides, so the messaging stays consistent across sales and marketing.

Perfect. Once you share the table, I will:
- Update the landing page copy and form helper text.
- Add a short example scenario for ecommerce brands.
- Adjust the premium finishes note placement and wording.

On the media side, I will reallocate 5 percent of the budget from social to search for the next 5 days and monitor how that affects quote volume and spec completeness in A7 and A8.

Sounds like a good plan. We will keep capturing feedback from new leads and can add more examples or clarifications to A4 and A8 if we see recurring questions.

For T11, I will continue logging insights so we have a richer view by the time we finalize the full post-launch report.

I will prepare the lead time and minimum order table today and add it to A3 and A8.

Once that is in place, it should be straightforward to reuse in the landing page and in A4.

Thanks everyone. I will incorporate these optimization steps into T12 and update A8 with:
- The current performance snapshot.
- The planned landing page and form changes.
- The small media reallocation toward search.
- The key customer insights from T11.

We can then review again after another week of data to see how these adjustments impact quote volume and spec completeness.
